meta.one_liner: Nasma sells handmade soy scented candles inspired by Alexandria's neighborhoods (Bahary, Sidi Gaber, El-Manshiya) — 180 EGP for a 220 g candle with a claimed 35-40 hour burn, sold on Instagram and WhatsApp with cash on delivery.
assumptions: Unattended run on a fictional product: the owner was not available for questions, so every gap was recorded here instead of being silently guessed.
The burn time (35-40 hours) is the owner's claim from the brief — not a documented burn test; the personas treat it as a claim.
Production cost and margin are unknown (wax, wicks, fragrance, jars) — the report makes no judgement on pricing viability.
Scent throw and room coverage are not in the brief — treated as an experience gap, not a fact.
The 100% soy claim has no test or certificate behind it — the brief says soy wax with no paperwork.
Whether the packaging survives summer shipping (soy wax in a delivery van) is unknown — the brief mentions no thermal protection.
Each persona's monthly income is an assumption (not in the brief); the 150-400 EGP gift budget is real, from the brief.
The announcement post was built only from the brief's facts (price, sizes, delivery, COD) with no invented offer — because this was an unattended run and no real post was handed over.
Test sales are near zero per the brief — treated as reality: zero documented reviews are available to the brand.

market.summary: Egypt's scented-candle market splits into three tiers: handmade premium (Aromatica — handmade in Cairo, 320-1250 EGP, shipping from 80 EGP, gift wrap 50 EGP), global mass (IKEA Egypt, 75 products from 49 to 449 EGP with strong seasonal discounts), and a quiet artisan tier (Creative Egypt lists a 410 EGP soy candle that is out of stock with zero reviews; noon Egypt carries a 400 g 100% soy candle by Tablowhaty, also out of stock with no listed price). Below all of it sit souq candles at 20-60 EGP per the owner's estimate. So there is a clear premium ceiling and a clear cheap floor, and the middle between them is exactly where Nasma sits — but that middle is also nearly empty of social proof: the research found no published reviews for any local artisan brand.

implications: Analysis: cost per burn hour favors Nasma — 180 EGP over a claimed 35-40 hours means 4.5-5.1 EGP/hour, cheaper than IKEA's 40-hour cup (219 = 5.5 EGP/h) and far below handmade premium (Aromatica's 350 g jar at 550). But the math only holds if the burn-time number is true — and that is a new brand's claim, not a published test.

Analysis: the budget skeptic does not see 'EGP/hour' first — he sees '180 = 3 souq candles (20-60 EGP)', a 3x to 9x gap on the same shelf. The brand has to run the correct math in public (a timed burn video) before the audience runs the wrong one.

Analysis: for gifts, a Nasma candle with wrap = 210 EGP versus the cheapest Aromatica gift = 320 + 50 wrap + 80 shipping, about 450. A strong deal for the gifter — missing only proof that the recipient will feel the value (brand plus the wrap experience).

Analysis: Cairo shipping at 45 EGP = 25% of the candle's price. Soy wax melts at fairly low heat (a known property of the material, assumed here) — summer shipping without documented thermal packaging can arrive warped, and that risk sits on 25% of the invoice.

feed.author: brand
feed.text: Nasma 🕯️ Handmade soy candles with the scents of Alexandria's neighborhoods — Bahary, Sidi Gaber, El-Manshiya. 220 g of soy wax + a cotton wick, a 35-40 hour burn, and the glass jar stays with you. Price: 180 EGP | The three-scent bundle: 480 EGP | Gift wrap (kraft + a handwritten card): +30 EGP. Delivery: Alexandria 25 EGP — Cairo 45 EGP. Cash on delivery. Order on Instagram or WhatsApp — production is limited because we make everything by hand.

feed.author: p3
feed.text: 180 EGP for a candle?! I buy 3 candles from the kiosk for 90 and still have change. 'Soy wax' is a grocery word they print on a label and people pay for it. Put up one lab sheet proving it is actually soy and I'll open the conversation.

feed.author: p1
feed.text: The scent idea is a ready-made gift in itself — 'Bahary' is the name of an Alexandria district; the recipient lives it instead of reading about it. I buy gifts every month and the cheapest handmade-brand gift starts above 450 with wrap and shipping. This one is 210 with the wrap. The number is very reasonable.

feed.author: p2
feed.text: Let me calculate instead of us getting emotional. 180 over 35-40 hours = 4.5-5.1 EGP per burn hour. IKEA's 40-hour cup = 219, that is 5.5 EGP/hour. So Nasma's price is cheaper per hour than the mass product itself. The only problem: who said 40 hours? The brand itself. No test, no video, no reference.

feed.author: p3
feed.text: That is my point. Every label says nice numbers. The 60 EGP souq candle claims 30 hours too, and nobody ever audited it. The real math is not 'EGP/hour' — the real math is: when does it actually burn out, and will you see it with your own eyes.

feed.author: p2
feed.text: Disagree. IKEA's number is factory-made with at least some QA. Nasma is a brand from zero — true. But the fix is not 'charge less'; the fix is publishing one documented test: a timelapse of a candle burning in front of a camera. One hour of content kills their biggest objection.

feed.author: p1
feed.text: Question for the brand: the 30 EGP wrap — what exactly is it? Kraft and a handwritten card is nice, but Aromatica charges 50 and the look is known. I am buying a gift, so the wrap is half the feeling. Show me a real photo of the wrap, not a design.

feed.author: p3
feed.text: And another thing: what does 'handmade' even mean in 2026? It means candle number 30 was made after number 29 and the batch varies. You are not buying a fixed product; you are buying a day in someone's life. That is not what these prices should be judged against.

feed.author: p1
feed.text: Exactly the opposite — that is the point. I am not buying a candle, I am buying a story to give: 'the scent of Sidi Gaber'. A factory candle never gives me a story.

feed.author: p2
feed.text: A serious point: Cairo delivery is 45 EGP. This is a soy candle, and soy melts at fairly low heat. July shipping in a delivery van from Alexandria to Cairo — what exactly arrives? A half-melted jar? Not one word in the post about thermal packaging or a replacement policy.

feed.author: p3
feed.text: And that is 45 EGP on a 180 price = 25% shipping. In plain words: you are charging 180 and receiving 135 of candle value, while unsure it arrives intact.

feed.author: p1
feed.text: A gift also means I do not test before sending — I am the buyer, not the user. If my friend opens it and hates the scent, there is no exchange and no refund. I carry the blame for the failed gift in front of people. I need something that kills that fear.

feed.author: p2
feed.text: That is a real gap, not noise. Suggestion: a 'one-time scent exchange' policy — the recipient swaps for another scent. It costs the brand one candle and buys far more trust.

feed.author: p2
feed.text: Who said 'Bahary' actually smells like the sea? Scent is the most personal thing there is. I once bought a 'sea and sand' candle from another brand and it was plain vanilla. 180 EGP on a scent I am not sure about + 45 shipping = an expensive experiment. Where are the samples? A mini bundle of the three scents?

feed.author: p3
feed.text: That is one point, not three. A candle is not an equation; a candle is an unknown until it is lit. 600 followers and not a single review, and you want me to prepay 180?

feed.author: p1
feed.text: Update: after thinking it over — I will try it. The three-scent bundle at 480 is exactly what I will do: each friend gets a scent, and I am done running out of flowers-and-perfume ideas. But I want two things confirmed first: real photos of the wrap, and a review from someone who actually bought.

feed.author: p2
feed.text: That review is the knot. You are asking for proof, and the brand has zero sales so far. The launch problem here is not the price — the price is sound. The problem is that there are no first 20 reviews building the bridge.

feed.author: p3
feed.text: Let me say something useful instead of grumbling: a candle that burns properly lasts longer if you trim the wick every time before lighting. Most people do not, so they burn the wax down a tunnel. If you are a serious brand, teach people — it cuts your returns and buys goodwill.

feed.author: p1
feed.text: An idea worth taking: if Nasma published scent profiles (who 'Bahary' suits, who 'El-Manshiya' suits) as content, those become choosing tools, not ads. If I need a gift for a sea person, I pick 'Bahary' because I understood it, not because the label was pretty.

feed.author: p2
feed.text: One small but important thing: 'the jar stays with you' — good, but nothing explains how to get the wax out at the end without scratching the glass. A 20-second video solves that too. This brand needs content, not a price fix.

feed.author: p3
feed.text: Last word: other brands say the same words. Aromatica says 'handmade in Cairo', charges 320, posts real photos and a known wrap. You are telling the same story for 180. Until something proves the words, I want evidence.

feed.author: p1
feed.text: Harsh but fair. I will pay the moment I see one real review — even from my groups. 600 followers is not proof; 6 reviews are the proof.

feed.author: p2
feed.text: To the brand: your price is sound (4.5-5.1 EGP/hour against IKEA's 5.5) — but there is no burn test, no summer-shipping protection, no scent samples, and no gift policy. Four near-zero-cost additions flip this post from curiosity to a purchase. It is not your price that is missing — it is the proof.

feed.author: p3
feed.text: The post's own best line: 'production is limited'. Fine — but limited needs paperwork: a photo of a real workshop, a batch at work, one face. Right now it reads like a magic shop — half the price of Aromatica, half the visibility.

feed.author: p1
feed.text: Summary: a full gift at 210 is a rare offer — the cheapest handmade brand is at about 450. I shared the photo in the group and three friends already liked the idea. All that is missing: one real review and one real wrap photo — and I order today.

feed.author: p2
feed.text: Today's summary for whoever is reading: Nasma is not overpriced — it is under-proven. 35-40 hours without a video, soy without paperwork, a wrap without photos, summer shipping without protection. Any one of those becomes real with one honest piece of content. On the other side: the Alexandria-neighborhood story is the sharpest edge in this market — nobody sells a district; they sell a brand.

objections.title: A brand new with zero reviews — 180 EGP prepaid is a bet, not a purchase
objections.suggested_fix: Before any marketing spend: turn the first 10-20 buyers (even neighbors and colleagues) into documented reviews with a short video and a photo of the delivered product — literally what the feed asked for ('6 reviews are the proof'). Handmade brands prove themselves with faces and photos, not sentences.
objections.validation_question: The last new brand you bought from on Instagram — what was the first thing that made you trust it?

objections.title: The burn time (35-40 hours) is an unverified claim — and the whole pitch rests on it
objections.suggested_fix: Burn one candle on camera as a timelapse and publish the real number on the post. One documented number wins the entire EGP/hour argument (4.5-5.1 against IKEA's 5.5) — and from there the post starts winning.
objections.validation_question: If a brand tells you the candle burns for 40 hours, do you trust the printed number or want to see it yourself?

objections.title: The skeptic's math: 180 = 3 souq candles (20-60 EGP) — a 3x to 9x gap on his usual shelf
objections.suggested_fix: Do not argue about the price — replace the math: 'a souq candle fades in 10-15 hours with no number; we publish our number per hour', and tie it to the documented test from o2. With the budget skeptic you win the calculation, not the sentence.
objections.validation_question: When did you last buy a candle, for how much — and how long did it actually burn?

objections.title: Cairo delivery at 45 EGP = 25% of the price — and a soy candle arriving in summer?
objections.suggested_fix: Test Cairo shipping yourself before offering it: send a candle to a Cairo address in peak heat (July-August) and inspect the state on arrival. If it needs thermal insulation (bubble wrap + a wax-safe box), price it in and say it explicitly in the post.
objections.validation_question: The last order that arrived warped or damaged by shipping — what did you do? Did you use the same service again?

objections.title: The gift buyer's risk: no testing before sending, no exchange policy
objections.suggested_fix: One written policy: 'Did not like the scent? A one-time exchange for another scent.' It costs a candle, and it buys the gifter's whole decision instead of pushing them to a pricier brand they already trust.
objections.validation_question: If you gifted a candle and your friend hated the scent — what would you want to happen?

objections.title: Scent throw is unknown: does 'Bahary' actually smell of the sea? And how much room does it cover?
objections.suggested_fix: Small trial samples (40-50 g of wax) of the three scents at 60-80 EGP with delivery inside Alexandria, or a trial bundle for the undecided. And publish a profile per scent (Bahary: who it suits) — the persona invented it in the feed.
objections.validation_question: Think of the last candle you used: was its scent strong enough for your room, or did it fade within half an hour?

objections.title: The gift wrap (+30) has no real photos — and it is the deciding point for the gift buyer
objections.suggested_fix: Publish 3-4 real photos of the wrap from every angle (kraft, the handwritten card, how it opens) in the post's archive. One real photo takes under an hour and decides a 210 EGP gift.
objections.validation_question: When you look at a brand's gift-wrap photos, what makes a real photo beat a design?

unspoken_objections.title: 'Soy' is a claim with no paperwork — and if it turns out to be a paraffin blend, the brand burns down once
unspoken_objections.why_it_might_exist: The 100% soy claim is common in the category (Tablowhaty says the same, s4) and no published test exists for any local brand. The skeptic raised it as a spark ('a grocery word') but never took it to its conclusion — one rumor in a WhatsApp group can kill a small brand completely.
unspoken_objections.validation_question: If a candle brand claimed '100% soy' and it turned out to be a blend — would you blame the brand or the whole market?

unspoken_objections.title: Handmade is not a feature in the audience's eyes — it is inconsistent quality
unspoken_objections.why_it_might_exist: The skeptic said it verbatim ('candle number 30 was made after number 29') — handmade means batch-to-batch variation, and the audience will not say it to the owner because it is an emotional point, not a technical one. First-batch defects (an off wick, a weaker scent) will arrive as individual complaints, not a public objection.
unspoken_objections.validation_question: If you bought a candle, loved it, and the second one had a weaker scent — how would you feel about the brand?

unspoken_objections.title: There is no summer plan: candles get bought in summer without anyone asking about shipping
unspoken_objections.why_it_might_exist: Not in the brief, and the research found no thermal-packaging signal in the local market. It stays unspoken because buyers only learn it from experience (a warped candle arrives) — and a persona already raised it ('soy melts') without a fix.
unspoken_objections.validation_question: Do you buy candles in summer? If your order arrives warped — do you blame the seller or the courier?

strengths.title: The Alexandria-neighborhood scent idea is a differentiation we found nobody else doing — Aromatica sells a scent; Nasma sells a district
A full gift at 210 EGP with the wrap sits inside the ready 150-400 budget — half the cheapest documented handmade brand (about 450)
Cost per burn hour favors Nasma (4.5-5.1) over documented factory mass (IKEA's 40-hour cup = 5.5)
Gift wrap at 30 EGP undercuts Aromatica's 50 — and adds one more sensory step to the brand

next_steps: Burn one candle on camera as a timelapse and publish the real burn hours — it kills the biggest blocker (o2) with a phone camera and one burn.
Take 3-4 real photos of the gift wrap from every angle and pin them in the Instagram archive — one hour of work that decides a gift (o7).
Trial samples: 40-50 g of wax in each of the three scents at 60-80 EGP with Alexandria delivery — opens the door for the undecided (o6).
Write a one-time scent-exchange policy for gifts and put it in the bio — the cost is one candle, the gain is full trust (o5).
Test Cairo shipping yourself in peak heat: send a candle to a Cairo address in July-August and inspect it on arrival before committing to the service (o4).
research_gaps: Jumia Egypt timed out twice — no scented-candle prices from the biggest local marketplace.
Amazon.eg returned 503 — unavailable for price research.
No published burn-hour standard or test exists in the local market — every burn figure (IKEA, Aromatica, Nasma) is the seller's claim.
No published customer reviews for any local artisan soy candle (Creative Egypt has zero) — social proof for the whole category is near zero.
Nasma's production cost and margin are unknown — any price advice here is market math, not a viability verdict.
No safety-certification information (wicks, thermal stability) for any local brand surfaced in the research.
The souq-candle estimate (20-60 EGP) is the owner's word, not a published source — it needs a quick check by walking a full souq.
The primary websearch tool was down (HTTP 402) for part of the run; research ran through DuckDuckGo HTML, so coverage may be thinner than a normal flow.
